near_miss.lead: tongue struck / cut (MIr. tengae ~ ON tunga with skera)
near_miss.why_not: Irish has a missile (erchor) striking the tongue of a man cursed by Moling; Norse has tongue cut out as punishment/martyrdom. Different events, no shared verb; body-part noun only.

near_miss.lead: kinship list athair, máthair, ingen, mac ~ matribus et patribus natos ~ pitaraṃ ... mātaraṃ
near_miss.why_not: Father+mother(+children) enumeration is universal and contexts differ (Irish: visitors who come to speak with the speaker each night; Lucretius: plague; AV: newborn not to harm parents). No figure beyond the basic kin terms.

near_miss.lead: water yields fish (usce ... iasc ~ vatn fullt af fiskum), fertility of land
near_miss.why_not: The Irish is the king's-truth/curse motif: water, wood and earth withhold fish, mast and fruit unless blood is paid. The Norse is a settlers noticing waters full of fish, with no royal or fertility frame. The Homeric good-king passage (Od. 19.109-114, recalled) has the motif but is not in the bundle and uses non-cognate words. Not claimable from the slab.
loch~lacus are cognate, but 'lake + waves' is ordinary description. Irish is onomastic lore about a red lake; Catullus greets Lake Garda. The wave words are not cognate.

near_miss.lead: Fer dá líach: father slain in battle, mother dead in childbirth; name given by parents (Od. μήτηρ τε πατήρ τε naming)
near_miss.why_not: The Irish explains a by-name from both parents' deaths. Homer has the name that mother and father call one; the Norse has a wife dead in childbed. These share kin terms and one theme each but no wording, and there is no Irish formula 'name that father and mother gave'.

near_miss.lead: apples carried over sea (Immram Máel Dúin) ~ Iðunn's apples
near_miss.why_not: Same noun (ubull ~ epli) in otherworld-ish contexts, but the narratives and syntax differ: the voyagers fill their boat with apples; Loki must bring Iðunn out of Ásgarðr with her apples. Thematic only, and the apple of immortality is widespread.

near_miss.lead: fasting (biad na dig) until told of one's mother and father
near_miss.why_not: Máel Dúin's fast to learn his parentage has no counterpart in the partners, which have only pitā mātā / matribus et patribus. The kin pair is generic.

near_miss.lead: futile act 'whispering to the deaf' (MIr. sanais fri bodar) with cognate *bʰodʰró- (bodar ~ badhira); cf. MBh 5.90 na tatra pralapet prājño badhireṣv iva gāyanaḥ
near_miss.why_not: The cognate pair is sound and the MBh simile (singing among the deaf, of futile speech) is congruent. But the slab partners use badhira in other senses (a ritual threat 'you will become deaf'; a list of blind, deaf and mad), and the speech verbs are not cognate. The proverb is near-universal (Lat. surdo canere/narrare), so independent coinage cannot be excluded. Same verdict for dall ... bodar ~ andha badhira lists (dall is not cognate).

near_miss.lead: wife of a living husband (Serb. женом иза жива мужа ~ Russ. у жива мужа жену)
near_miss.why_not: An exact shared Slavic collocation (*žena *živa mǫža, taking a wife from her living husband), but both witnesses are Slavic, so the two-branch anchoring rule fails. The Irish pivot (a cleric bringing fish, wine and wheat) is unrelated. It is probably Common Slavic or a later legal-moral cliché, not demonstrably PIE.

near_miss.lead: life without death till Doomsday (bethaid gan écc co bráth) ~ dīrgham āyuḥ
near_miss.why_not: The Irish is Christian hagiographic idiom (co bráth = till Judgment), and its words are not cognate with the Vedic long-life formula.

near_miss.lead: washing at/with water (MIr. nigid ... uisce ~ Gk νίζω ... ὕδατι, *neigʷ- + *wed-)
near_miss.why_not: The verbs are cognate and both have water. But in the Irish the Morrígan washes with one foot at each side of the river (fri husci = by the water), while the Greek is instrumental 'wash with water' (a wound, or the hands before crossing a river). 'Wash with water' is too generic to be diagnostic.

error.correct_reading: gáet, pret. pass. 3sg of gonaid 'wounds, slays' (< *gʷʰen-)
error.evidence: context: t'athair ... gaet in fer i car h [OCR for i cath], marb in ben dot breith 'the man was slain in battle, the woman died at your birth'

error.correct_reading: breith (vn of beirid), 'dot breith' = at your birth
error.evidence: parallel 'dia breith' in context line; c for e
'lotair for muir' = 'they went on the sea'. It is not loitid 'destroys'.

error.correct_reading: for (preposition 'on'); î is a misread f
uisce, dat. sg. with h-prothesis ('fri husci' = beside the water); same word as husce later in the line
error.evidence: parallel 'fri husce antuaith' in the same sentence
'cona tibridis usce a iasc ... talam a thorad' = that water would not give its fish ... nor earth its fruit

error.correct_reading: aingel is a loan from Latin angelus (Gk ἄγγελος), so it has no native PIE etymon
error.evidence: standard loanword; 'aingil do nimh' = an angel from heaven

note: Second reading of 12 flagged bundles. No claims: every lead is generic, thematic-only, non-cognate, or single-branch (Slavic 'wife of a living husband'). The strongest, sanais fri bodar ~ badhireṣv iva gāyanaḥ (MBh 5.90), is logged as a near-miss.
